placeholders.percentText: the download percentage, already formatted (for example 42%)
placeholders.downloaded: bytes downloaded so far, already formatted for display (for example 1.2 GB)
placeholders.total: total download size, already formatted for display (for example 2.0 GB)
placeholders.speed: current download speed without the unit suffix, already formatted (the /s suffix is added separately)
placeholders.eta: the formatted time-remaining string (for example 35s), or the literal none when no estimate is available yet

ai.cloudConsent.askCmdr.contentsRule: Cmdr never sends whole files, photos, or thumbnails. When you ask about a file, it can read a limited part of it: some lines of text, a few pages of a PDF along with its title and author, the list of files inside an archive, or a photo’s camera details, including where it was taken. Photo search works the same way: the text Cmdr recognized inside the matching photos and their tags go to your provider so it can find them. Cmdr can suggest renames, moves, and cleanups, and nothing happens to a file until you approve it.

@ai.cloudConsent.askCmdr.contentsRule.description: Now shown under Settings > AI > Provider, in the Allow cloud AI fold, as a reassurance paragraph after the Ask Cmdr list. Four facts to keep: whole files, photos, and thumbnails are never sent; when the user asks about a file, the assistant reads a limited part of it (some lines of text, a few PDF pages plus the PDF's title and author, the names of the files inside an archive, a photo's camera details including where it was taken); photo search sends the text recognized inside the matching photos and their tags; and the assistant proposes file changes but never carries one out without the user approving it. Must NOT promise that no file contents are sent, and must NOT promise that the assistant changes nothing (it writes its own notes and proposes renames and moves). The apostrophes are U+2019.
@ai.cloudConsent.askCmdr.contentsRule.screenshotNote: AI feature copy. Cloud-connection states, suggestions, and translate-errors surface around the Settings > AI > Provider subsection pictured here (and inline near AI actions). This shows the AI provider settings for context.

ai.cloudConsent.askCmdr.memory: Cmdr writes itself notes about you: how you like things organized, what you’ve turned down before, anything you ask it to remember. Those notes ride along with every message you send, for as long as they exist, and they can include text Cmdr recognized inside your photos. You can read them, or wipe them, any time in the Ask Cmdr settings.

@ai.cloudConsent.askCmdr.memory.description: Now shown under Settings > AI > Provider, in the Allow cloud AI fold, as a paragraph after the Ask Cmdr list, about the assistant's memory: it writes notes about the user, those notes go to the provider with every message for as long as they exist, they can contain text recognized inside the user's photos, and the user can read or delete them in the Ask Cmdr settings. Keep all four facts. The apostrophe is U+2019.
@ai.cloudConsent.askCmdr.memory.screenshotNote: AI feature copy. Cloud-connection states, suggestions, and translate-errors surface around the Settings > AI > Provider subsection pictured here (and inline near AI actions). This shows the AI provider settings for context.

ai.cloudConsent.askCmdr.proactive: Cmdr also watches the folders you use and starts a conversation when it has something to suggest, so messages can reach your provider without you asking first. You can turn that off in the Ask Cmdr settings, under “On its own”.

ai.secretError.keychainTitle: {op, select, save {Couldn’t save your API key: macOS Keychain denied access} other {Couldn’t read your saved API key: macOS Keychain denied access}}

@ai.secretError.keychainTitle.description: Title of an error shown in the cloud-AI provider settings (Settings > AI cloud, and the onboarding cloud-provider step) when saving or reading the API key fails because the macOS Keychain refused access. "macOS Keychain" and "Keychain" are the proper name of the Apple credential store; keep them as Apple names them in your language (Apple ships a localized Keychain Access app, so use that localized name). Write each branch as a complete, natural sentence in your language rather than a shared prefix plus a clause.

placeholders.op: which action failed: "save" when storing a new key, anything else when reading the stored key

@ai.secretError.keychainTitle.screenshotNote: AI feature copy. Cloud-connection states, suggestions, and translate-errors surface around the Settings > AI > Provider subsection pictured here (and inline near AI actions). This shows the AI provider settings for context.

ai.secretError.keychainBody: {op, select, save {Open Keychain Access and check the “Cmdr” entry, or delete it and try saving again.} other {Open Keychain Access, find the “Cmdr” entry, grant access, or delete it and re-enter your key.}}

@ai.secretError.keychainBody.description: Guidance shown below the macOS-Keychain-denied error in the cloud-AI provider settings, telling the user how to fix it via Apple’s Keychain Access app. "Keychain Access" is the proper name of the macOS app (Apple ships it localized; use that localized name). “Cmdr” is the app name (a Keychain entry label) and must NOT be translated. Write each branch as a natural full sentence.

placeholders.op: which action failed: "save" when storing a new key, anything else when reading the stored key
